WEATHER WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 34 · AGES 4–5

Shadows — solve it right on the sheet.

Compare shadow lengths, match shadows to the time of day, circle the shadow maker and trace SHADOW.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then match, circle, count, trace and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

← Seasonal Foods and HarvestPrevious activitySnowy Weather and Winter Clothes →Next activity
HOW TO DO IT

Five little steps.

  1. 1

    Compare

    Circle the longer shadow in each pair.

  2. 2

    Match

    Match each tree shadow to its time of day.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Circle the thing that makes a shadow.

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the shadow shapes and write the totals.

  5. 5

    Trace

    Trace the big word SHADOW, then draw the tree's shadow.

Ask a grown-up to read the steps aloud the first time. After that, you know just what to do.

YOUR PENCIL CASE

Pick your tools.

Pencil, nine crayons, an eraser, undo, redo and clear — the tools appear right here and work on the sheet. Save keeps your finished work as a picture, and your saved work comes back next time.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: A shadow is the dark copy light makes when something stands in the way — and it moves with the sun.

Knowledge to have ready: Long and short, morning-noon-evening, and the rule that light makes shadows happen.

Why this activity matters: Shadows are a child's first experiment they can run with their own body — the sheet formalises what the garden already shows.

  • Shadow logic
  • Time-of-day matching
  • Counting
  • Tracing and writing
  • Prediction

What to say before you start: Light makes a dark copy of everything it meets. Let us catch some shadows on paper.

What to look for on the sheet: For the flashlight in the circle row — it makes shadows without the sun, and that is a discovery.

Questions to ask along the way: Why is the morning shadow long and the noon shadow short? Where is yours right now?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Long shadow means low sun — say it once, then let the sheet prove it.

Parent tips: Pencil, torch and a toy on the table turn the last box into a live experiment.

Understanding check: What do you need to make a shadow? Two things, no paper.

Real-life practice: Trace each other's shadows with chalk at noon and again after tea.
